summary: Solution-processable transport-layer inks for perovskite solar cells.
editor_note: Perovskite manufacturing has a materials bottleneck hiding behind its efficiency charts. Sofab sells Tinfab and Nicfab inks: its SnO2 layer has produced cells above 20% efficiency and stays stable for over two years, while its NiOx layer is claimed to be three times more durable than PTAA. Unlike a lab-only recipe, the bet is coating-compatible chemistry customers can order and test. The risk is whether those results survive module-scale qualification and volume production.
tags: perovskite solar,materials science,solar manufacturing,thin films,climate tech

product_evidence.claim: Sofab says Tinfab is a solution-processable SnO2 electron-transport layer that supports PIN and NIP architectures, multiple coating methods, and cells above 20% efficiency.
The Tinfab page says the ink remains stable for more than two years and is available as an orderable sample rather than only as a laboratory formulation.
Sofab says its tunable NiOx Nicfab layer is three times more durable than PTAA and has produced an 18% efficient full-metal-oxide cell.

market_context.primary_user: Perovskite cell developers, solar manufacturers, and materials teams qualifying transport layers for scalable coating processes.
market_context.differentiation: Sofab packages tin-oxide and nickel-oxide transport layers as stable, orderable inks compatible with multiple deposition methods instead of leaving them as lab recipes.
market_context.why_now: Perovskite commercialization increasingly depends on repeatable materials and module-scale manufacturing, not another record-efficiency cell in isolation.

risks.claim: The falsifiable risk is whether reported cell efficiency and durability translate into module-scale yield, customer qualification, and high-volume production economics.
risks.basis: VentureDex editorial assessment from the official Tinfab, Nicfab, and funding evidence.
